title: Deep learning method for wear assessment and regeneration support in gear hobbing tools

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Cutting tools are indispensable components in machining and manufacturing, as they directly determine surface quality, dimensional accuracy, and overall process efficiency. Among them,  gear hob cutters  play a key role in the gear manufacturing industry, where gears are formed through a continuous generating process known as gear hobbing. Due to their complex helical geometry, tight tolerances, and the use of advanced tool materials, gear hobs are among the most sophisticated and costly cutting tools in production engineering (Choudhury & El-Baradie,  6 ; Hodgyai et al.,  10 ; Watson,  38 ). Consequently, extending their operational lifespan is both an economic and technological necessity (Munaro et al.,  22 ).

During machining, cutting tools are subjected to continuous mechanical and thermal loads that gradually degrade their cutting edges and functional surfaces. This phenomenon, referred to as  tool wear , arises primarily from abrasive, diffusion, oxidation, and fatigue mechanisms acting at the tool–workpiece interface. These wear processes progressively alter the cutting geometry and material integrity, leading to deteriorated surface finish, reduced dimensional accuracy, and loss of process efficiency (Cheng et al.,  4 ; Zhou et al.,  40 ).

For this reason, cutting tools undergo regeneration processes-such as re-sharpening, re-coating, and re-grinding-which enable multiple reuses of the same tool body. These procedures effectively lower production costs, reduce material waste, and promote sustainable manufacturing practices (Koshy et al.,  17 ; Shaw,  31 ). From an industrial perspective, efficient tool regeneration is a critical factor in cost optimisation and production reliability, directly linking tool condition monitoring with process sustainability and overall manufacturing competitiveness (Mohamed et al.,  21 ). In this context, an accurate and reliable evaluation of tool wear prior to regeneration is essential to ensure restoration quality and to maximise the service life of cutting tools. This evaluation can be performed using either direct or indirect methods.

Indirect methods enable the estimation of cutting tool wear through the analysis of process related signals such as cutting forces, vibrations, acoustic emissions, temperature, or spindle power. A wide range of studies have explored these approaches, including research on acoustic emission and vibration analysis (Bhuiyan et al.,  2 ; Snr,  32 ; Teti et al.,  35 ), power consumption monitoring in machine tools (Jemielniak,  13 ), infrared thermography (Saatçı et al.,  28 ), and cutting force measurement (Jáuregui et al.,  12 ; Jemielniak & Arrazola,  14 ). The primary advantages of such methods include their non-intrusive nature and the possibility of seamless integration with machine tools, enabling real-time process supervision. However, their main drawbacks lie in limited flexibility-each cutting condition typically requires separate calibration, and signal interpretation strongly depends on the workpiece material, lubrication state, and cutting environment-as well as relatively low robustness to process disturbances.

Direct methods rely on visual or microscopic examination of tool wear regions, such as the flank, rake, and cutting edge surfaces. Common approaches include employing optical instruments such as toolmaker’s microscopes and workshop magnifiers, which provide sufficient resolution for evaluating wear (Čerče et al.,  3 ). More advanced techniques are also used, including dedicated CCD camera systems (Loizou et al.,  19 ; Peng et al.,  23 ), Focus-Variation microscopy, scanning electron microscopy (Liu et al.,  18 ; Vučina et al.,  37 ), or 3D optical scanners (Valigi et al.,  36 ). These methods provide very high precision in both classification and dimensional quantification of worn areas, while simultaneously capturing detailed information about surface morphology and topography. However, these approaches remain largely manual and exhibit limited inspection throughput, which makes a complete evaluation of the cutting tool a highly time-consuming process.

Given the rapid advancement of machine learning and computer vision technologies, their integration with industrial inspection systems has attracted considerable research interest. In particular, deep learning methods have been successfully applied to defect detection, fault diagnosis, and wear assessment tasks, often outperforming traditional rule-based image processing approaches in terms of robustness and adaptability.

For semantic segmentation problems related to tool condition monitoring, many recent solutions are based on encoder–decoder architectures derived from U-Net (Gao et al.,  8 ; Schlager et al.,  29 ; Schlegel et al.,  30 ). Such approaches have demonstrated strong performance in identifying wear-related regions and other manufacturing defects, with reported IoU values exceeding 0.9 in controlled application scenarios. Recent studies have also explored attention mechanisms, feature-fusion strategies, and lightweight network designs to improve performance under limited data availability and computational constraints (Sun et al.,  33 ; Tao et al.,  34 ).

For the specific case of gear cutting tools, Kamratowski et al. recently presented a vision-based framework for wear detection and quantification aimed at supporting tool regeneration decisions (Kamratowski et al.,  16 ). By comparing conventional image-processing techniques with a deep learning segmentation model based on a U-Net architecture with an EfficientNet backbone, the authors demonstrated accurate localisation and dimensional assessment of worn regions. Their results highlighted the potential of learning-based approaches for supporting industrial wear inspection while simultaneously indicating the importance of computational efficiency and robustness for practical deployment.

Nevertheless, the study also identified several limitations, including sensitivity to variations in illumination and surface reflections, which may adversely affect segmentation reliability under industrial conditions. In addition, the relatively high computational complexity of the proposed architecture highlights the need for more lightweight and computationally efficient solutions suitable for large-scale deployment. It is also worth noting that although the presented vision-based method could be readily integrated with image acquisition systems, it was not embedded within a broader, end-to-end automated tool inspection framework. This observation indicates a gap remaining in the development of integrated inspection systems that combine acquisition, analysis, and decision support for practical industrial use.

In summary, the authors identify a clear need for a dedicated, automated inspection system designed specifically for the evaluation of gear hobbing tools. Such a solution should form part of a broader framework for tool condition monitoring and regeneration planning, enabling seamless integration with industrial maintenance workflows. To be successful in production environments, the applied machine vision and machine learning methods must demonstrate high robustness to variable environmental conditions, such as illumination, focus, or surface contamination, ensuring consistent performance under real-world industrial settings (Marciniak et al.,  20 ; Rolih et al.,  26 ). Furthermore, the system should exhibit low computational complexity, ensuring fast and reliable operation on standard hardware (Chen et al.,  5 ).

In response, the authors present a vision-based inspection system for the evaluation of gear hob cutters, designed as an operator-assistance tool to support wear estimation and regeneration decision-making. The key highlights of the study are as follows: enhanced wear segmentation stability and spatial consistency through the formulation of a compound loss function integrating Binary Cross Entropy (BCE), Dice–Sørensen, Focal Tversky, Isolation Penalty, and Total Variation terms, perturbation analysis under simulated variations (illumination, focus, and contamination), providing an initial assessment of framework resilience against environmental acquisition variances within adopted operational ranges, a multi-stage vision pipeline coupling a YOLO12-based defect detector with a custom lightweight segmentation architecture (Ghost Slim U-Net), integration of automated image acquisition, defect detection, wear segmentation, and dimensional wear quantification within a unified inspection framework. scan-level data aggregation with visualisation-driven operator support to streamline wear tracking and assist consistent tool regeneration decisions.

sections.heading: Problem definition
paragraphs: Cutting tools are fundamental components in machining operations, as they directly engage with the workpiece to remove material through shear deformation. However, during operation, they progressively deteriorate due to friction, elevated temperature, and cyclic mechanical stresses. This phenomenon-known as  tool wear -manifests in several characteristic forms, including flank wear, crater wear, notch wear, and adhesion or diffusion effects, each influencing cutting performance differently (Cheng et al.,  4 ; Colantonio et al.,  7 ). Progressive wear leads to a deterioration of surface finish, dimensional accuracy, and overall machining efficiency.

The present study focuses on a specific class of cutting tools -  gear hob cutters . In industrial practice, these tools undergo periodic  regeneration  to restore their cutting capability. The simplest and most common regeneration method involves the removal of material from the front (rake) face of the cutting tooth-commonly referred to as  re-sharpening from the tooth face . This process effectively re-establishes the cutting edge geometry but requires precise determination of the material allowance to be removed (known as the  stock removal allowance ). Grinding is performed in successive vertical rows (i.e., along the tool axis), which means that the wear for each row must first be estimated. The final regeneration allowance is determined by the maximum wear observed among all rows. It is not feasible to apply different allowances for individual rows, as the grinding process must preserve geometric uniformity and axial alignment across the entire tool profile (Hodgyai et al.,  10 ).

Wear defects can be categorised not only by their visual morphology but also by their practical impact on the regeneration process. Some forms-such as uniform flank wear-are predictable and allow straightforward correction. Others, such as notch wear or edge chipping, are irregular and may compromise tool integrity, while minor adhesion or surface contamination generally do not affect machining performance but can hinder defect detection (Astakhov,  1 ). Given this variability, accurate and repeatable wear estimation is essential. Manual inspection, though common, is time-consuming, subjective, and prone to inconsistency, particularly when dealing with fine or subtle wear patterns. In contrast, an intelligent, vision-based system leveraging deep learning can automatically assess wear distribution, detect anomalies, and reduce gross human errors in measurement or judgment. Such a system can support operators by providing objective, quantitative input for regeneration decisions-specifically, determining the appropriate stock removal allowance.

Consequently, there exists a strong need for an  operator-assisted ,  intuitive , and  computationally efficient  wear estimation system that seamlessly integrates into the industrial workflow. For gear hob cutters, such a solution enables rapid and reliable determination of wear and regeneration parameters, enhancing precision, efficiency, and decision confidence while minimising the risk of critical misestimations.

sections.heading: Defect catalogue
paragraphs: Building upon the need for reliable and automated assessment of tool condition, a dedicated catalogue of surface anomalies was developed to support systematic analysis and model training. Each anomaly type was characterised in terms of its visual appearance, repeatability, and frequency of occurrence throughout the tool’s operational lifecycle. The resulting catalogue serves both as a reference for the operator and as a foundation for supervised learning and quantitative evaluation of wear patterns.

In total, four primary categories of surface anomalies were identified: Flank wear:  the most common wear type, characterised by predictable and repeatable depth, occurring exclusively on the flank face. Notch wear:  material loss caused by brittle fracture at the cutting edge or tooth sides, exhibiting irregular geometry and unpredictable depth. Built-up edge:  adhesion of machining material fragments to the cutting edge, extending beyond the nominal tooth perimeter. Although easily removed during sharpening, such deposits may obscure other defects. Contamination:  foreign material deposited on the tool surface. The identified anomalies were subsequently analysed with respect to their structural characteristics, regeneration relevance, and mutual similarity. Large instances of  notch wear , such as complete tooth breakouts, were excluded from the dataset, as they manifest as missing surface regions and cannot be reliably represented in image-based analysis.

Considering established industrial practice, and acknowledging that the boundary between edge wear and minor forms of surface degradation is often ambiguous and requires expert interpretation in a given process context, the defect classes  flank wear  and minor  notch wear  located at the cutting edge were merged into a single class denoted as  edge wear . The size and morphology of this consolidated class have a direct and dominant influence on regeneration decisions, as the entire affected region must be removed during the re-sharpening process.
As a result, three final defect classes were defined for the purposes of this study:  edge wear ,  built-up , and  contamination .

sections.heading: Automatic data acquisition
paragraphs: The studies presented in this work were inspired by real industrial needs and conducted with a focus on practical applicability. Consequently, the image acquisition system was developed using a heavily modified VENTURION 600 V420E measurement system (ZOLLER GmbH & Co. KG, Germany). The existing kinematic configuration of the device, consisting of motorised  X  and  Z  linear axes and rotational  C -axis, enabled precise and rapid positioning of the tool as well as a fully automated scanning process.

To minimise the influence of the industrial environment on image acquisition, as well as the impact of the acquisition process on the surroundings, the vision system employed illumination outside the visible spectrum. A long-pass optical filter with a 750 nm cutoff was mounted on the lens, effectively blocking the visible spectrum and transmitting infrared wavelengths. Illumination was provided by two infrared LEDs (centre wavelength 850 nm) installed at a large angle relative to the camera’s optical axis in a dark-field configuration. This arrangement enabled imaging of defects on the surfaces of the tool teeth. The lighting system was designed symmetrically, allowing observation of teeth orientated both to the left and to the right. For visual preview and preparatory operations prior to scanning, additional bright-field illumination using identical light sources was employed.

The station was equipped with a PC and monitor, allowing the operator not only to initiate and supervise the scanning procedure, but also to review and edit the acquired results. Although the image acquisition process itself is fully automated, the operator is required to provide basic information about the inspected tool, either manually or by following the steps of an interactive wizard, and to perform system referencing using the first complete tooth located at the top of the tool. The required tool parameters include: Number of rows (number of teeth along the circumference of the tool), Number of sections (number of teeth along the tool axis), Pitch diameter, Tool height, Lead direction, Module. Based on these parameters, the system determines the positions of subsequent teeth and automatically executes the image acquisition sequence.

At the beginning of the procedure, the camera is positioned at a suitable distance along the  X -axis to ensure proper focus. Subsequently, by means of vertical movements along the  Z -axis and rotational movements of the tool around the  C -axis, the system sequentially positions the camera relative to individual teeth and acquires the corresponding images.

The acquired images, together with a mapping file containing their spatial coordinates in the machine coordinate system, are stored on disk for further processing in subsequent stages of the pipeline.

sections.heading: Prepared dataset
paragraphs: The dataset was constructed from 50 scans of cutting tools, encompassing both upper and lower relief surfaces. The scans were acquired from 21 distinct tool instances under varying tool conditions, including immediately after machining, after coating removal, and after regrinding. In accordance with the industrial practice of the expert partner, the study was limited to a selected group of  gear hob cutters  characterised by similar geometry and comparable wear behaviour resulting from their operating conditions. Consequently, the presented dataset was regarded as adequately representative for the intended validation objectives, encompassing the key operating conditions and variability relevant to the considered industrial context. The experimental design was therefore considered suitable for assessing the proposed methodology within its defined application scope.

Edge wear regions and additional surface anomalies, such as built-up edge formations and surface contamination, were annotated using polygonal masks. The final dataset consisted of 2500 annotated images containing: 2487 instances of  edge wear , 563 instances of  built-up , 579 instances of  contamination . Representative examples from the dataset are presented in Fig.  2 .

The analysis of polygon shape and spatial distribution, illustrated in Fig.  3 , reveals clear differences between the edge wear annotations and the remaining defect classes. Edge wear polygons are characteristically long and narrow, forming slender structures that are consistently localised within a well-defined image region corresponding to the cutting edge of the tooth scan. In contrast, surface artefacts such as contamination and built-up material exhibit more irregular geometries. Built-up material tends to cluster in close proximity to the edge wear regions, particularly on their left-hand side corresponding to the relief face of the tool, whereas contamination instances are predominantly distributed across the remaining tooth surface to the right of the cutting edge. Fig. 3 Analysis of defect size and spatial distribution within the image. All reported dimensions are normalised with respect to the image size. The red dashed line indicates the approximate location of the cutting edge

A 5-fold cross-validation protocol was employed for all experiments conducted in this study. The prepared dataset was partitioned into five equal subsets at the scan level rather than the image level. These subsets were subsequently used to train and validate five independent models. Such a strategy ensured that images originating from the same tool instance and wear condition were not simultaneously present in the training, validation, and test sets, thereby reducing the risk of data leakage and overly optimistic performance estimates caused by correlated samples. The exact distribution of defect class instances across the prepared cross-validation folds is presented in Table  1 . All results reported in the following sections are presented as the arithmetic mean and standard deviation across the evaluated folds. sections.heading: Proposed processing pipeline
paragraphs: The processing of data acquired during tool scanning is divided into three main steps, as illustrated in Fig.  4 : (1)  image processing , in which each input image is analysed to detect surface anomalies, resulting in bounding boxes for contamination and built-up regions, as well as polygon-based segmentation of  edge wear ; (2)  defect analysis and measurement , where dimensional wear measurements are performed individually for each tooth based on the detected  edge wear  regions; and (3)  results post-processing and visualisation , in which scan-level filtering, aggregation, and visualisation of the obtained results are carried out. At each stage, data are exchanged with the database, as the workflow utilises not only the acquired images but also operator-provided information describing the inspected tool. Fig. 4 Overview of the proposed scan data processing and visualisation pipeline for supporting tool regeneration decisions

sections.heading: Image processing
paragraphs: In the first step of the proposed pipeline, each image is processed individually. Given the characteristics of the input images described in Subsect. “ Prepared dataset ” and the need for precise determination of wear values, the authors proposed decomposing the image processing step and employing two deep learning models (Fig.  5 ).

The raw input image acquired from the scanning machine undergoes initial pre-processing consisting of alpha correction with a factor of 1.5 to enhance image contrast, followed by gamma correction with a factor of 1.75 to normalise illumination. After this step, the image is vertically cropped; the cropping value is determined by the pitch of the cutting tool and remains constant within a single scan. Subsequently, the tooth surface image is downscaled to the target resolution and passed to the first detector, whose task is to identify and locate both  edge wear  defects and other surface defects ( contaminations  and  built-ups ). Fig. 5 Diagram of of the proposed two-stage image processing method

The bounding boxes of the detected  edge wear  defects are filtered, and the largest one is used to define the Region of Interest (ROI) for the semantic segmentation stage, while the remaining detections are stored in the database. The ROI is extracted from the image at its original resolution and then rescaled to match the input size of the segmentation model. The resulting segmentation mask is subjected to contour extraction and filtering, and the final polygon is stored in the database. The entire image analysis procedure is executed in a loop and repeated for all images acquired during the scanning of the tool.

sections.heading: Defect analysis and measurement
Results post-processing and visualisation
paragraphs: Finally, the system suggests the grinding allowance as the maximum wear value detected for the given tool. After verification and possible modification by the operator, this value, together with the remaining data obtained during the scan, is used to generate a report containing information about the tool parameters, its current condition, and the recommended reconditioning method, supplemented with a time–cost analysis.

sections.heading: Deep learning models
paragraphs: As the primary defect detector, the authors employed the YOLO12s object detection model (Jocher et al.,  15 ), based on the YOLO (You Only Look Once) architecture (Redmon et al.,  25 ), which is characterised by its compact size (9.3 million parameters) and high inference speed. The input image resolution was set to 960 px. The model hyperparameters and the data augmentation methods applied are described in Appendix A.

As the  edge wear  segmentation model, the authors proposed a modified U-Net architecture (Ronneberger et al.,  27 ), referred to as the  Ghost Slim U-Net  (Fig.  7 ). The proposed architecture integrates Ghost Convolutions, a reduced number of channels (8 instead of the standard 64), and an additional filtering layer. Ghost Convolution blocks replace standard 2D convolutions by first generating a compact set of intrinsic feature maps via a primary convolution, followed by lightweight depthwise operations that produce complementary “ghost” feature responses (Han et al.,  9 ). Although these lightweight operations effectively reduce model complexity, their dependence on a small number of intrinsic filters and linear feature synthesis can limit feature diversity and increase sensitivity to shifts in input distributions. To mitigate this, standard convolution blocks were retained in the first two encoder stages, increasing representational redundancy and frequency coverage at the input level, thereby ensuring that a broader set of stable features is captured and propagated through deeper layers. A new bottleneck module was designed to improves the stability of learned representations while preserving robustness to distribution shifts and maintaining a low computational overhead. The primary convolutional block is responsible for feature extraction, whereas an additional residual component based on global spatial averaging introduces a weak, channel-dependent contextual signal. This mechanism enhances the presence of informative features without altering their spatial localisation and functions as an auxiliary regularisation mechanism. Fig. 7 Diagram of developed Ghost Slim U-NET

sections.heading: Model preparation
Annotation analysis
paragraphs: The  edge wear  annotations used in this study were created in accordance with operational guidelines provided by the industrial partner collaborating on the deployment of the inspection system. Consequently, the definition of edge wear reflects established industrial practice applied during tool qualification for regeneration rather than a formal metrological standard.

To assess annotation consistency, an additional experiment involving two independent annotators was conducted on a randomly selected subset of 100 images. For each corresponding pair of segmentation masks, the Jaccard index (IoU) was calculated. Representative examples are shown in Fig.  8 . Fig. 8 Comparison of segmentation masks independently produced by two expert annotators, illustrating annotation variability

These values provide an approximate reference level associated with annotation variability and operational ambiguity. Consequently, the dimensional errors reported for the evaluated segmentation models should be interpreted relative to this practical consistency level.

sections.heading: Experimental setup and system validation
paragraphs: To evaluate the proposed image processing method, a series of experiments were designed to validate its individual components: the defect detector, the  edge wear  segmentator, and the complete system.

Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) were used as metrics of wear quantification error. These metrics directly assess the accuracy of the estimated edge wear values and therefore reflect the performance of the complete processing pipeline, encompassing segmentation, post-processing, and final wear quantification. As such, they provide a comprehensive evaluation of the final output of the system, namely the edge wear measurement used to support regeneration decisions.

The experimentation, including the training of the machine learning models as well as the validation of the system, was carried out locally on a workstation equipped with an Intel Xeon Silver 4110 CPU (Intel Corporation, USA), 64GB RAM and an Nvidia RTX 4080 graphics card with 16GB VRAM (NVIDIA Corporation, USA).

sections.heading: Ablation study of the compound loss components
Evaluation of the Ghost Slim U-Net architecture
paragraphs: To evaluate the proposed architecture, it was compared against selected efficient image segmentation models, namely: Vanilla U-Net, SegFormer-B0 (Xie et al.,  39 ), Fast-SCNN (Poudel et al.,  24 ), YOLO12n-seg instance segmentation model (nano variant). All non-YOLO models were trained using the proposed compound loss function. This experimental design enables a direct comparison between the proposed method, classical U-Net-based approaches, and lightweight segmentation architectures.

sections.heading: End-to-end system evaluation
paragraphs: In the case of the overall system evaluation, validation was performed for the complete processing pipeline, from ROI extraction to final wear quantification. This experiment enabled the assessment not only of individual module performance, but also of their interoperability, robustness to error propagation, and overall system reliability under realistic operating conditions. The experiment was conducted using the  Ghost Slim U-Net  model trained with the compound loss function.

sections.heading: System robustness analysis
paragraphs: To evaluate the robustness of the proposed system, additional experiments were conducted under controlled variations in image acquisition conditions. Three types of perturbations were considered: (i) Gaussian blur to simulate defocus, (ii) gamma correction to model illumination changes, and (iii) synthetic contamination and built-up regions (Fig.  9 ). Fig. 9 Examples of introduced synthetic perturbations at different intensity levels (images cropped for visualisation purposes)

The robustness study evaluates the stability of  edge wear  segmentation under these controlled disturbances, which are commonly used proxies for variability in industrial vision systems. It should be emphasised that these synthetic perturbations do not fully represent all sources of variability in real production environments, but provide a reproducible framework for comparative analysis (Huang et al.,  11 ).

Performance degradation was quantified using the MAE of wear quantification as the primary metric, while the area under the performance curve (AUC) was computed to summarise overall stability under increasing disturbance levels. This aggregated measure enables a relative comparison of methods within a controlled evaluation setting.

sections.heading: Ablation study of the edge wear segmentator
System robustness analysis
paragraphs: The results of the robustness analysis are presented in Fig.  10 . The selected models were evaluated under three types of artificially introduced anomalies: gamma modification, gaussian blur, and simulated contaminations. Fig. 10 Results of the robustness evaluation for different models in the  edge wear  segmentation and measurement task under varying acquisition conditions (e.g., illumination, focus, and surface contamination)

Despite being designed primarily for computational efficiency, Ghost Slim U-Net maintained stable segmentation performance across the considered perturbation scenarios. Compared with other lightweight architectures, including YOLO12n-seg and Fast-SCNN, the proposed model generally exhibited lower performance degradation under increasing disturbance levels. Fig. 11 Results of the robustness evaluation for compound and BCE loss function in the  edge wear  segmentation and measurement task under varying acquisition conditions (e.g., illumination, focus, and surface contamination

This observation suggests that the additional structural constraints introduced by the Compound Loss contribute to maintaining more stable segmentation outputs in the presence of localised image disturbances. This behaviour is particularly relevant for contamination-related artefacts, including built-up regions that may partially obscure wear boundaries. Although the analysis was performed using synthetic perturbations, the results indicate improved robustness of the proposed loss formulation under the considered contamination scenarios.

It should be noted that the performed robustness analysis is based on controlled synthetic perturbations and therefore represents a comparative evaluation framework rather than a comprehensive assessment of real-world industrial variability. Furthermore, robustness to acquisition-related disturbances should not be interpreted as robustness to domain shifts arising from changes in tool geometry, coating type, or wear mechanisms. Addressing such cases would require the acquisition of representative data and subsequent model adaptation.

Nevertheless, the obtained results indicate that the proposed  Ghost Slim U-Net  architecture maintains competitive segmentation performance under the considered perturbation scenarios while preserving high computational efficiency. Similarly, the proposed Compound Loss consistently reduced performance degradation under contamination-related disturbances, suggesting improved robustness within the scope of the evaluated conditions.

sections.heading: End-to-end system evaluation
paragraphs: These results suggest that image-level anomaly detection can provide useful contextual information for operator-assisted inspection, although its reliability is limited by the small spatial extent and sparsity of the considered defects. In particular, minor contaminations often occupy only a few pixels, which increases sensitivity to image resolution and annotation precision. While higher-resolution imaging or more complex detection architectures could potentially improve performance, such modifications would also increase computational cost, which is a relevant constraint in large-scale scanning workflows.

The average processing time was 95 ms per image. This consisted of first-stage defect detection and post-processing (61.2 ms), second-stage segmentation and post-processing (28.8 ms), and edge wear quantification (4.9 ms). The timing analysis indicates that the first-stage defect detector (YOLO12s) constitutes the largest computational component of the pipeline. Consequently, further reductions in processing time may be achievable through the adoption of a more computationally efficient detection architecture, analogous to the optimisations introduced in the segmentation stage.

sections.heading: Measurement outlier analysis
paragraphs: In general, performance degradation is more pronounced for extreme wear geometries and irregular cutting-edge conditions.

Further qualitative analysis of selected high-error cases (Fig.  13 ) provides additional insight into these failure modes. In Fig.  13 A, a representative case is shown where a substantial built-up (residual adhered workpiece material) is incorrectly segmented as edge wear. In Fig.  13 B and C, the model identifies the main wear region, but smaller elongated built-up structures are partially merged with the segmentation mask. These cases highlight the difficulty of separating wear from contamination when they co-occur spatially.

These observations highlight a limitation of fully automated interpretation in scenarios involving complex surface conditions. In the proposed workflow, the system therefore provides visual and quantitative outputs intended to support operator review, including detailed wear maps and auxiliary defect detections. Additional scan-level filtering and inspection tools are available to assist in identifying ambiguous or corrupted measurements, as described in Section “ Results post-processing and visualisation ”.

sections.heading: Scan-level inspection results
paragraphs: To investigate the influence of post-processing on error reduction, three scan-level filtering strategies were evaluated: (i) automatic outlier removal using interquartile range (IQR) analysis, (ii) optional operator-assisted removal of a small fraction of high-error predictions (top 2%), enabled by the proposed visualisation module, and (iii) a hybrid approach combining both methods.

In the subsequent step, the processing time required for a complete tool scan was analysed. The total processing time, including file input/output operations and SQL database communication but excluding acquisition system latency, amounted to 10 min 20 s for a representative tool comprising 812 cutting teeth. This corresponds to an average processing time of approximately 760 ms per tooth, with image processing requiring 95 ms per image. The reported result was obtained using a sequential processing scheme, in which individual tooth images were processed one at a time. Further reduction of processing time may be achievable through parallelisation of independent processing steps, enabling simultaneous analysis of multiple teeth.

The main time constraint in the overall workflow appears to be the image acquisition stage. The currently used  move-stop-capture  mode significantly increases data collection time. A continuous acquisition strategy with constant rotational speed could potentially reduce this overhead and improve overall throughput, although its practical implementation would require synchronisation with the imaging system. Fig. 14 Visualisation of tool wear (edge wear) in  A  3D cylindrical representation and  B  2D flat representation

The conducted analysis indicates that the application of automatic filtering methods, complemented by optional operator intervention, may improve scan-level measurement consistency. The proposed system provides dedicated visualisation and data inspection tools that enable such a workflow.

In this setup, operator involvement is shifted from manual inspection of individual cutting edges to the review of aggregated digital measurement results. Although this may change the nature of the interaction with the data, the overall workflow remains semi-automated, with the operator initiating the scan and subsequently validating the generated outputs.

Compared with traditional manual inspection, which relies on direct visual assessment of each cutting edge, the proposed approach reduces the need for low-level inspection tasks by focusing operator attention on higher-level interpretation of computed results (e.g., Fig.  14 ).

The combination of system-generated measurements and domain expertise supports structured decision-making regarding tool condition assessment and regeneration planning, while limiting the influence of purely subjective visual evaluation.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: This study presented a vision-based inspection framework for gear hob cutter evaluation, integrating defect detection, wear segmentation, and wear quantification within a unified processing pipeline. The proposed approach investigated the applicability of deep learning methods for supporting tool regeneration workflows through more consistent and repeatable wear assessment.

The obtained results suggest that the proposed pipeline can support semi-automated wear assessment in industrial inspection workflows. However, the presented study should be regarded as a feasibility investigation performed on a limited industrial dataset. The proposed approach remains constrained by annotation subjectivity, the resource-intensive data acquisition process, and the limited representation of tool geometries, coatings, and wear mechanisms available in the current dataset.

Future work will focus on expanding the dataset with additional industrial cases and performing validation on a broader range of wear mechanisms and tool configurations. Particular attention will be devoted to synthetic data generation and simulation-based approaches, including physically based rendering environments, to improve data diversity, scalability, and model generalisation.
